summary: Actual causation, explanation, responsibility and blame have formal concept-level definitions in structural causal models: HP actual cause (AC1-AC3, three variants), Halpern's explanation as a sufficient cause relative to an epistemic state with goodness and explanatory power, Chockler-Halpern responsibility 1/(k+1) and blame as expected responsibility, Beckers' sufficient and counterfactual explanations, Miller's contrastive explanation, Halpern-Kleiman-Weiner intention. Correct explanations of a classifier's output are defined (Chockler-Halpern, ReX, Watson's PN/PS). No work defines faithfulness of a verbalized rationale, self-explanation or CoT as actual causation; the nearest are PNS scores for CoT steps (Yu et al. 2025) and PN/PS for LLM reasoning. One framework could cover faithfulness, completeness, plausibility (explanation relative to the reader's epistemic state) and graded step responsibility: HP actual causality, lifted to LLMs via Halpern-Pass's model-free abstraction and Beckers' nondeterministic causal models.

candidates.title: Causes and Explanations: A Structural-Model Approach, Part I: Causes
candidates.venue: British Journal for the Philosophy of Science (arXiv cs/0011012)
concepts: counterfactuals as used to test explanations
candidates.formalism: structural causal models (structural equations, causal settings (M,u))
candidates.formal_object: When a conjunction of primitive events X=x is an actual (token) cause of an event phi in a causal setting: but-for dependence under a contingency W=w', a sufficiency clause, and minimality.
candidates.key_formula: AC1: (M,\vec u)\models(\vec X=\vec x)\wedge\varphi.\ AC2: \exists (\vec Z,\vec W),\ \vec X\subseteq\vec Z,\ (\vec x',\vec w'):\ (a)\ (M,\vec u)\models[\vec X\leftarrow\vec x',\vec W\leftarrow\vec w']\neg\varphi;\ (b)\ (M,\vec u)\models[\vec X\leftarrow\vec x,\vec W'\leftarrow\vec w',\vec Z'\leftarrow\vec z^*]\varphi\ \forall\vec W'\subseteq\vec W,\vec Z'\subseteq\vec Z.\ AC3: \vec X\ \text{minimal}. (updated definition, as restated in the appendix of Part II)
candidates.assumptions: A known, fully specified (recursive) causal model with chosen endogenous/exogenous variables and a known context; verdicts are model-relative.
candidates.relevance: The base definition the user plans to build on: a faithful CoT could be one whose stated reasons are actual causes of the answer; AC2's contingencies handle redundant/backup reasoning paths that defeat plain but-for (deletion) tests.

candidates.title: Causes and Explanations: A Structural-Model Approach. Part II: Explanations
candidates.venue: British Journal for the Philosophy of Science (conference version IJCAI 2001; arXiv cs/0208034)
candidates.formalism: structural causal models + epistemic state (set K of contexts, optionally a probability)
candidates.formal_object: An explanation of phi relative to the contexts K an agent considers possible: a minimal X=x that is a sufficient cause of phi wherever it holds in K and is not already known; plus partial explanations and explanatory power.
candidates.key_formula: EX1: (M,\vec u)\models\varphi\ \forall\vec u\in\mathcal K;\ EX2: \vec X=\vec x\ \text{is a sufficient cause of}\ \varphi\ \text{in}\ (M,\vec u)\ \forall\vec u\in\mathcal K\ \text{with}\ (M,\vec u)\models\vec X=\vec x;\ EX3: \vec X\ \text{minimal};\ EX4: (M,\vec u)\models\neg(\vec X=\vec x)\ \text{for some}\ \vec u\in\mathcal K\ \text{and}\ (M,\vec u')\models\vec X=\vec x\ \text{for some}\ \vec u'\in\mathcal K
candidates.assumptions: Known causal model (or a set of candidate models in the general version), an explicit epistemic state K of the explainee, a prior Pr for partial explanations.
candidates.relevance: Gives a formal notion of explanation that is relative to the explainee's knowledge; this suggests separating faithfulness (explanation w.r.t. the LLM's true model) from plausibility (explanation w.r.t. the reader's model). Sufficiency is a candidate formalization of completeness.

candidates.title: Actual Causality
candidates.formalism: structural causal models, normality orderings, probability over causal settings
candidates.formal_object: Three variants of HP actual causation (original, updated, modified), graded causation via normality, degree of responsibility and blame, explanation as sufficient cause relative to an epistemic state, partial explanations with goodness (alpha,beta) and explanatory power.
candidates.key_formula: \text{Explanatory power (Def. 7.2.5)}:\ \Pr(\mathcal K(\vec X=\vec x,\varphi,\mathrm{SC2})\mid[\![\vec X=\vec x]\!]);\quad db(\mathcal K,\Pr,X=x,\varphi)=\sum_{(M,\vec u)\in\mathcal K}dr((M,\vec u),X=x,\varphi)\Pr((M,\vec u))
candidates.assumptions: Known causal model or a probability over causal settings; choice of variables matters (model relativity, Ch. 4); normality ordering if graded causation is used.
candidates.relevance: The reference for every definition the user needs: the modified HP definition (lowest complexity), graded responsibility and blame, explanatory power, and the book's own treatment of how to choose variables, which an LLM application must justify. Local copy in actual-causality/.

candidates.title: Responsibility and blame: a structural-model approach
candidates.formalism: structural causal models + epistemic state (probability over causal settings)
candidates.formal_object: Degree of responsibility of X=x for phi: 1/(k+1), with k the minimal number of variables that must change to make phi counterfactually depend on X=x; degree of blame: expected responsibility over an agent's epistemic state.
candidates.key_formula: dr((M,\vec u),(X=x),\varphi)=0\ \text{if}\ X=x\ \text{is not a cause of}\ \varphi;\ \text{else}\ \tfrac{1}{k+1},\ k=\min\#\{W\in\vec W:\ w'_W\neq W(\vec u)\}\ \text{over witnesses}\ ((\vec Z,\vec W),(x',\vec w'))\ \text{satisfying AC2}
candidates.assumptions: Known causal model and context for responsibility; a probability over causal settings (the agent's epistemic state) for blame.
candidates.relevance: The standard graded notion: could grade how much each CoT step or verbalized factor is responsible for the answer, and blame could separate what a model 'could have known' (relevant to intent and sandbagging arguments).

candidates.title: A Modification of the Halpern-Pearl Definition of Causality
candidates.formalism: structural causal models
candidates.formal_object: Modified HP definition: contingency variables W are frozen at their actual values; simpler, handles Hopkins-Pearl problems, lower complexity (D_1^P) than the original and updated definitions.
candidates.key_formula: AC2(a^m):\ \exists\vec W\subseteq\mathcal V\setminus\vec X,\ \vec w^*,\ \vec x':\ (M,\vec u)\models\vec W=\vec w^*\ \wedge\ (M,\vec u)\models[\vec X\leftarrow\vec x',\vec W\leftarrow\vec w^*]\neg\varphi\ \text{(as restated in Halpern and Pass 2025, Def. 2.1)}
candidates.assumptions: Known causal model and context.
candidates.relevance: The variant Halpern currently prefers; freezing contingencies at actual values maps naturally onto 'hold the rest of the CoT/activations as they were' interventions.

candidates.title: Causality Without Causal Models
candidates.formalism: abstract counterfactual structures (Lewis/Stalnaker-style), modal logic of counterfactuals
candidates.formal_object: An abstract HP-style definition of actual cause (and of explanation) for any model with counterfactuals; causes and effects may be arbitrary formulas, including disjunctions, negations, beliefs and nested counterfactuals; allows backtracking.
candidates.assumptions: A counterfactual structure (closeness/selection function) and a chosen set C_X of allowable contingency formulas; no structural equations needed.
candidates.relevance: Removes the need for an explicit SCM over CoT tokens and allows causes that are beliefs or formulas, which a definition of 'the stated reason caused the answer' or of self-report accuracy needs.

candidates.title: Causal Explanations and XAI
concepts: counterfactuals as used to test explanations
candidates.formalism: structural causal models
candidates.formal_object: Weak, direct and strong sufficiency; sufficient explanations (X=x,N) with a safeguarded network N; counterfactual explanations as contrastive analogs; actual causation defined from good sufficient explanations.
candidates.key_formula: (\vec X=\vec x,\vec N)\ \text{is a sufficient explanation of}\ Y=y\ \text{iff}\ \vec X=\vec x\ \text{is strongly sufficient for}\ Y=y\ \text{along}\ \vec N:\ Y\in\vec N\ \wedge\ \forall\vec c\in R(\vec C),\vec u:\ (M,\vec u)\models[\vec X\leftarrow\vec x,\vec C\leftarrow\vec c]\vec N=\vec n,\ \vec C=\mathcal V-(\vec X\cup\vec N)
candidates.assumptions: Known causal model of the inputs and the ML model's output; the explanation must name which variables are safeguarded from interventions.
candidates.relevance: Formal account of when an explanation of an ML output is correct and action-guiding; distinguishes kinds of sufficiency that matter for whether a CoT's reasons 'suffice' for the answer (completeness) and gives counterfactual explanations a causal semantics.

candidates.title: Large Language Models as Nondeterministic Causal Models
concepts: counterfactuals as used to test explanations
candidates.formalism: nondeterministic causal models
candidates.formal_object: A semantics for counterfactuals of probabilistic LLMs by representing an LLM as a nondeterministic causal model; contrasts it with the Gumbel-max deterministic SCM representation of Chatzi et al. and Ravfogel et al.
candidates.assumptions: Black-box access to the LLM's conditional output distribution; no implementation details needed.
candidates.relevance: Supplies the missing step for applying HP to LLMs: a principled causal model of the LLM itself, so that 'had the CoT/prompt been different, the answer would have been...' is well defined.

candidates.title: Causal Sufficiency and Necessity Improves Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
candidates.authors: Xiangning Yu, Zhuohan Wang, Linyi Yang, Haoxuan Li, Anjie Liu, Xiao Xue, Jun Wang, Mengyue Yang
concepts: counterfactuals as used to test explanations
candidates.formalism: probabilities of causation (Pearl) over an SCM of CoT steps
candidates.formal_object: Probability of sufficiency of a reasoning chain and probability of necessity / PNS of an individual CoT step for the correct answer, with identifiability results; used to prune or add steps.
candidates.key_formula: PN(S,s_t,q)=P\big(A_{do(s_{<t},\bar s_t,s'_{>t})}\neq y\mid A=y,S,q\big);\quad PNS(S,s_t,q):=P(A_S=y,\ A_{S'}\neq y),\ S'=(s_{<t},\bar s_t,s'_{>t})
candidates.assumptions: Answer is a function of the CoT; interventions replace a step with a corrupted variant and regenerate later steps; correct answer known.
candidates.relevance: The only work found that applies counterfactual necessity/sufficiency to CoT steps; targets correctness and efficiency rather than faithfulness, and uses Pearl's PN/PS, not HP actual causation (no contingencies).

candidates.title: Explaining Image Classifiers
candidates.formalism: structural causal models (Halpern 2016 explanation)
candidates.formal_object: Halpern's explanation (necessity and sufficiency clauses, restriction of options considered) applied to a classifier's output; shows Mothilal et al. use a stronger condition; covers explanations of absence and of rare events.
candidates.assumptions: The classifier is the causal model; input features (pixels/regions) are the variables; a set of contexts the agent considers.
candidates.relevance: Shows how to instantiate HP explanation for a learned model's output and where popular XAI definitions deviate from it; a template for defining what a correct explanation of an LLM answer is.

candidates.title: Causal Explanations for Image Classifiers
candidates.authors: Hana Chockler, David A. Kelly, Daniel Kroening, Youcheng Sun
candidates.venue: Journal of Artificial Intelligence Research, vol. 86, 2026
candidates.formalism: actual causality and causal responsibility
candidates.formal_object: Black-box explanations of image classifier outputs grounded in actual causality; approximate explanations with proven termination, complexity and approximation bounds (tool ReX).
candidates.assumptions: Black-box query access; a masking/occlusion baseline defines interventions.
candidates.relevance: The main working implementation of HP explanation plus responsibility ranking for neural models; shows how to approximate the definition at scale.

candidates.title: Sufficient, Necessary and Complete Causal Explanations in Image Classification
candidates.formalism: actual causality; logic-based (abductive) explanations
candidates.formal_object: Sufficient and necessary causal explanations, their equivalence to logic-based explanations, and delta-complete / 1-complete explanations (explanation classified with at least a given confidence).
candidates.assumptions: Black-box access; classifier confidence available.
candidates.relevance: Gives formal causal notions of sufficiency, necessity and completeness of an explanation, which map onto the completeness and soundness requirements in the user's scope.

candidates.title: Probabilities of Causation: Bounds and Identification
concepts: counterfactuals as used to test explanations
candidates.formalism: structural counterfactuals / potential outcomes
candidates.formal_object: Probability of necessity (PN), sufficiency (PS) and both (PNS) of a binary cause for a binary effect, with sharp bounds from experimental and observational data.
candidates.assumptions: Binary variables (extensions possible); a structural model; identification needs exogeneity/monotonicity or bounds.
candidates.relevance: The probabilistic counterpart of but-for causation used by every PN/PS-based CoT and rationale paper; a population-level alternative when HP's token-level setting is too fine for stochastic LLMs.

candidates.title: Local Explanations via Necessity and Sufficiency: Unifying Theory and Practice
candidates.authors: David Watson, Limor Gultchin, Ankur Taly, Luciano Floridi
candidates.formalism: probability over a context distribution; logic of factors; causal interventions optional
candidates.formal_object: A basis (f, D, C, ordering); probability that a factor is sufficient / necessary for an output; tau-minimal sufficient factors; unifies SHAP, anchors and counterfactuals; sound and complete algorithm LENS.
candidates.key_formula: PS(c,y):=P(f(z)=y\mid c(z)=1);\quad PN(c,y):=P(c(z)=1\mid f(z)=y),\ z\sim\mathcal D
candidates.assumptions: A target function, a context distribution D (observational or interventional), a set of candidate factors.
candidates.relevance: Shows that common XAI explanations are necessity/sufficiency claims relative to a context distribution; the choice of D is exactly the choice of counterfactual inputs in CoT faithfulness tests.

candidates.title: Contrastive Explanation: A Structural-Model Approach
concepts: counterfactuals as used to test explanations
candidates.formalism: structural causal models (extends Halpern 2015)
candidates.formal_object: Contrastive counterfactual cause and contrastive bi-factual cause: answers to 'why phi rather than psi' as pairs of partial causes differing minimally.
candidates.key_formula: \langle\vec X=\vec x,\vec X=\vec y\rangle:\ CC1\ \vec X=\vec x\ \text{partial cause of}\ \varphi\ \text{in}\ (M,\vec u);\ CC2\ (M,\vec u)\models\neg\psi;\ CC3\ \exists\vec W,\vec w:\ \vec X=\vec y\ \text{partial cause of}\ \psi\ \text{in}\ (M_{\vec W\leftarrow\vec w},\vec u);\ CC4\ (\vec X=\vec x)\cap(\vec X=\vec y)=\emptyset;\ CC5\ \vec X\ \text{maximal}
candidates.assumptions: Known causal model; an explicit foil psi.
candidates.relevance: Formalizes the contrastive questions behind counterfactual faithfulness tests (why answer A rather than B) within HP; the formal follow-up of Miller's 2019 survey.

candidates.title: Towards Formal Definitions of Blameworthiness, Intention, and Moral Responsibility
candidates.formalism: structural causal models + epistemic state (probability over causal models) + utility
candidates.formal_object: Degree of blameworthiness and intention relative to an epistemic state (a probability over causal models and a utility on outcomes); combined with actual causality to give moral responsibility.
candidates.assumptions: The agent's probability over causal models and utility function must be specified or inferred.
candidates.relevance: An HP-based formal definition of intention, relevant to scheming, covert goals and sandbagging; links intent to actual causation, which a causal account of hidden objectives could reuse.

candidates.title: Actual Causation and Nondeterministic Causal Models
candidates.formalism: nondeterministic causal models
candidates.formal_object: A definition of actual causation in nondeterministic causal models, built from generalized counterfactual dependence and structural simplification; verdicts close to Beckers 2021/2022.
candidates.assumptions: A nondeterministic causal model; applies to deterministic models as a special case.
candidates.relevance: Actual causation for stochastic mechanisms, which sampled LLM reasoning is; pairs with Beckers' LLMs-as-nondeterministic-models paper as a route to HP-style token causation for CoT.

candidates.title: Gumbel Counterfactual Generation From Language Models
candidates.authors: Shauli Ravfogel, Anej Svete, Vésteinn Snæbjarnarson, Ryan Cotterell
concepts: counterfactuals as used to test explanations
candidates.formalism: structural equation model via the Gumbel-max trick
candidates.formal_object: Reformulates an LM as a structural equation model with Gumbel sampling noise, giving a joint distribution over an observed string and its counterfactual under an intervention; hindsight Gumbel sampling infers the noise.
candidates.assumptions: Access to next-token logits; the Gumbel-max representation of sampling (contested by Beckers 2025).
candidates.relevance: Makes rung-3 counterfactuals of LLM generations computable, so HP-style conditions ('holding the sampling noise fixed, had step t differed') can be evaluated on real CoTs.

candidates.title: Towards Trustworthy Explanation: On Causal Rationalization
candidates.authors: Wenbo Zhang, Tong Wu, Yunlong Wang, Yong Cai, Hengrui Cai
candidates.formalism: structural causal model of rationalization; probabilities of causation
candidates.formal_object: A structural causal model of rationale selection and probabilities of causation (necessity and sufficiency) of text snippets, with identification, used to learn non-spurious, efficient rationales.
candidates.assumptions: Proposed SCM of rationalization; identification conditions; extractive rationales of text classifiers.
candidates.relevance: The closest NLP use of causal necessity/sufficiency to define a correct (non-spurious) rationale; extractive rather than generated, so it does not cover verbalized CoT.

candidates.title: Explaining Black-Box Algorithms Using Probabilistic Contrastive Counterfactuals
candidates.authors: Sainyam Galhotra, Romila Pradhan, Babak Salimi
concepts: counterfactuals as used to test explanations
candidates.formalism: probabilistic contrastive counterfactuals (probabilities of causation) over a causal diagram
candidates.formal_object: Necessity, sufficiency and necessity-and-sufficiency scores of attribute values for a black-box decision, at local, contextual and global levels, plus recourse (system LEWIS).
candidates.assumptions: A causal diagram over inputs (or background knowledge), identification of counterfactual probabilities.
candidates.relevance: Replaces associational 'responsibility' scores in XAI with probabilities of causation; a population-level graded alternative to Chockler-Halpern responsibility.

candidates.title: Explanation in Artificial Intelligence: Insights from the Social Sciences
candidates.formalism: none (semi-formal survey of philosophy and psychology)
candidates.formal_object: Semi-formal: explanations are contrastive, selected, social, and causal rather than statistical. Formal definitions build on it, notably Miller 2021 (contrastive explanation in SCMs).
candidates.relevance: Influential semi-formal framework recorded because formal contrastive definitions build on it; useful for separating what humans find explanatory (plausibility) from what is causally correct.

candidates.title: Does Reasoning Emerge? Examining the Probabilities of Causation in Large Language Models
candidates.formalism: probabilities of causation (PN, PS)
candidates.formal_object: Conditions under which an LLM's approximations of PN and PS for a reasoning problem can be computed and compared to the true mechanism, as a test of whether LLMs reason.
candidates.assumptions: A known ground-truth causal mechanism (math problems); LLM treated as an abstract machine with a natural-language interface.
candidates.relevance: Applies PN/PS to LLMs, but to the correctness of reasoning about a world model, not to whether stated reasoning causes the output.

candidates.title: Slaying the Hydra: Interaction-Aware Circuit Discovery in Language Models
candidates.authors: Sankaran Vaidyanathan, Rafal Urbaniak, Emily Bunnapradist, Michelangelo Naim, Daniel Waxman
candidates.formalism: actual causality (witnesses) with expectations over cause and witness sets
candidates.formal_object: Witness-integrated set effect (WISE), causal estimands that average HP-style witness contingencies over sets of components, used to rank LM components for circuit discovery.
candidates.assumptions: White-box access to model components; interventions on activations.
candidates.relevance: Brings HP witnesses (contingencies) to LLM internals, addressing backup components that defeat one-at-a-time ablation; the same issue arises for redundant CoT steps.

gaps: Faithfulness of CoT, self-explanations and self-reports: no definition as actual causation (stated reasons are actual causes of the output) found; existing CoT work uses Pearl PN/PS or intervention sensitivity without HP contingencies.
Post-hoc rationalization: no formal definition in the actual-causation literature (it would be an explanation that is sufficient in the reader's model but not an actual cause in the model's).
Plausibility: not formalized as such; Halpern's epistemic explanation relative to an explainee's set K is a candidate but no paper uses it this way.

Completeness and soundness of natural-language explanations: formal only for feature-set explanations (Halpern sufficiency, Beckers strong sufficiency, Kelly-Chockler delta-completeness), not for generated text.
Mapping verbalized reasoning to causal variables: no account of which variables a CoT step denotes; it needs causal abstraction or Halpern-Pass formula-level causes.
Graded responsibility of individual CoT steps or verbalized factors: no application of Chockler-Halpern responsibility or blame found.
Monitorability, obfuscation, steganography, honesty and simulatability: no definitions in this literature.
